taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes S. magister is treated as a full species with ongoing gene flow to S. bimaculosus and S. uniformis, which some treat as subspecies; a BLM Red Rock Canyon leaflet lists the yellow-backed spiny lizard as S. uniformis.
fieldMarks: Stout, strong-looking lizard 3.25-5.5 inches (Zion key; 3.25-6 in per Saguaro NPS).
Gray to brown mottled with yellow, green, brown and metallic blue; black shoulder markings.
Males have iridescent blue along the sides and belly and more orange and yellow than Clark's spiny lizard; large overlapping scales.
Underside of the tail has black bars (Zion key).
behavior: Active about April-May to September-October in the north; more comfortable on ground and rocks than on trees.
Shelters under rocks or in rodent burrows; eggs laid in soil.
Eats mainly insects and spiders, sometimes centipedes, lizards and plant material.
Two clutches a year in Utah; hatchlings appear from July in Texas.
habitat: Arid and semiarid plains and lower slopes: desert shrubland and woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, juniper-mesquite woodland, arroyos, playa edges and cottonwood-willow river zones.
Occurs on trees, rocks and the ground near cover.
range: Nevada and southwestern Colorado south to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Coahuila; west of the Central Valley in California and east to western Texas; near sea level to about 1,520 m.

lookalikes.name: Clark's spiny lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Found at higher elevation, often in trees; black and white stripes on the forelimbs (Tuzigoot NPS page).
